articles.body_html:
What behavioral science reveals about engagement loops, digital habits, and the responsibility of developers.

The software that doesn't want you to leave

You open an app to check one thing: whether a package shipped, what time the game starts, a reply from a friend. You find it in seconds. Then a post below it catches your eye, and another below that, and when you next look at the clock twenty minutes have gone somewhere you never decided to send them.

Nothing malfunctioned. The feed did precisely what it was built, tuned and measured to do, and those twenty minutes were logged somewhere as a small engineering success.

Software can be excellent at meeting its engagement objectives while producing experiences that conflict with what its users wanted from their time. What happens when software succeeds at keeping us engaged but fails to respect our original intentions?

Engagement in itself is not the problem. Reading a long essay, learning a language or a video call with family are engagement too. The useful distinction is between engagement a person would endorse on reflection and engagement they drift into and later regret.

Public conversation tends to land on the individual. In a July 2026 segment of NPR's TED Radio Hour, journalist Nayeema Raza proposed that three pre-internet habits could help people slow down and break the screen cycle. Personal habits matter, but every habit plays out in an environment, and on a screen that environment is written by developers. This essay looks at that side of the glass.

The architecture of engagement

Almost every feature associated with compulsive use began as a fix for a real problem. Infinite scrolling removed the friction of pagination on small touchscreens. Autoplay spares someone watching a series from reaching for the remote. Notifications tell you a person needs you. Recommenders find the few relevant items among millions. Streaks help people keep up practice they chose.

What these features share is that they remove a decision point. A paginated list ends, and the end is a natural moment to ask whether you want more. Each convenience shortens the distance between continuing and never having decided at all.

Reviewing 43 papers, Monge Roffarello, Lukoff and De Russis catalogued eleven types of what they call attention-capture damaging patterns, infinite scroll and autoplay among them. They distinguish deceptive designs, which mislead, from seductive ones, which deceive no one and simply make continuing the path of least resistance. Most engagement features are of the second kind, which is why intent is a poor guide to their effects.

In a survey of 120 YouTube users, Lukoff and colleagues found that autoplay and recommendations primarily undermined people's sense of agency, while search and playlists supported it. That is self-reported perception, not measured harm, but it shows that one product can contain features that hand control to the user and features that quietly take it back.

Underneath the interface sits the objective function. A ranking model trained on watch time or click-through rate learns to serve whatever produces those signals. Kleinberg, Mullainathan and Raghavan formalized the difficulty in a theoretical model in which users have an impulsive in-the-moment self and a long-term self with different preferences, while the platform observes only behavior. In their model, raising engagement improves welfare along some directions of design change and lowers it along others, and engagement data alone cannot reveal which. It is a model rather than an empirical finding, but it names the core problem: behavioral data measures what people do, not what they wanted.

What behavioral science actually tells us

The science here is more interesting and less alarming than the popular version.

Habits. Wood and Rünger's review describes habits as responses that, through repetition in stable contexts, come to be triggered by cues rather than deliberate goals. They are an efficient default mode of action, with a curious side effect: people tend to infer from how often they do something that they must have intended it. Software that sits one tap away in every idle moment is well positioned to become such a cue.

**Uncertain rewards. **Since Skinner's operant conditioning research, psychologists have known that behavior rewarded intermittently tends to persist longer than behavior rewarded every time. A feed mixes things you care about with things you do not, in an unpredictable order, which is why HCI researchers, Rixen and colleagues among them, have discussed partial reinforcement as a plausible explanation for scrolling's pull. It is a plausible hypothesis built on an analogy to laboratory findings, not an established mechanism of feed use.

Dopamine and the word "reward." In 1997, Schultz, Dayan and Montague showed that the activity of dopamine neurons in monkeys matched a reward prediction error, the quantity at the heart of temporal-difference learning algorithms. That paper bridged machine learning and neuroscience, and it has been stretched far beyond what it shows. The signal it describes concerns learning, the updating of expectations, rather than pleasure, and nothing in those recordings establishes that every notification releases dopamine in your brain.

The shared vocabulary causes its own confusion. In a recommender trained with reinforcement learning, "reward" is a number an engineer chose, such as a click or seconds watched, and "learning" means updating parameters. In psychology and neuroscience, the same words describe how organisms' behavior and neural activity change with experience. The mathematics overlaps; the mechanisms differ. What genuinely connects them is the behavioral loop: the system learns what you respond to while you learn what the system delivers. Two learners, coupled through an interface.

Attention. The experimental evidence on interruptions is clearer. In a laboratory study, Stothart, Mitchum and Yehnert found that merely receiving a call or text notification, without answering it, impaired performance on an attention-demanding task. In a randomized field experiment with 237 smartphone users, Fitz and colleagues found that people whose notifications were batched three times a day felt more attentive, productive and in control, and reported better mood, than controls. Hourly batching did little, and no notifications at all brought more anxiety and fear of missing out. The lesson concerns timing and dose, not abolition.

**Self-regulation. **In an experience-sampling study of 205 adults, Hofmann, Vohs and Baumeister found that desires for media use, along with work, brought about the most self-control failure. A randomized experiment by Allcott, Gentzkow and Song offers stronger evidence. Temporarily paying people to use social media less reduced their use even after the payments stopped, consistent with habit formation, and letting people set limits on their own future use reduced it substantially, suggesting they wanted to use less than they did. Through their economic model, the authors estimate that self-control problems account for 31 percent of social media use: a model-based estimate, but resting on an experimental pattern that is hard to dismiss.

The trouble with "addiction." None of this licenses calling ordinary use an addiction. Reviewing the literature, Panova and Carbonell found insufficient support for smartphone addiction as a disorder and proposed "problematic use" instead. Kardefelt-Winther and colleagues warned that the behavioral-addiction label is being stretched until it pathologizes ordinary leisure.

"Screen time" deserves similar caution. Across three large datasets, Orben and Przybylski found that digital technology use explained at most 0.4 percent of the variation in adolescent well-being; Twenge, Haidt and colleagues contested that reading, and the debate remains open. Meanwhile, a meta-analysis by Parry and colleagues found that self-reported media use correlates only moderately with logged use, and problematic-use scales even more weakly. Total minutes is a blunt instrument. What people do, why, and whether it crowds out the rest of their lives tell us far more.

Why willpower is only part of the equation

If behavior were purely a matter of resolve, interface design would be irrelevant. The Fitz study is a quiet rebuttal: participants did not become more disciplined; their environment changed, and their experience changed with it.

A useful way to see this is to count actions. In a continuous feed, continuing costs nothing, while stopping requires a decision nothing in the interface prompts. In a batched design, continuing costs one deliberate action and stopping costs none. Neither forces anything; they differ in which choice is the default.

A field study by Rixen and colleagues shows how rarely the app itself provides the exit. Tracking 46 participants' social media sessions for a week, they found that most reasons for ending a session had nothing to do with the app: a waiting task, sleep, food, another person. Sessions spent mainly scrolling were rated less positively than those spent mainly posting or watching stories, though individual differences mattered far more than session content.

It is tempting to conclude that friction is the answer. The evidence is more modest. A large meta-analysis of choice-architecture interventions by Mertens and colleagues, subsequently corrected by its authors, reported an average effect, but a reanalysis by Maier and colleagues found no evidence of an overall effect after correcting for publication bias, a disagreement still unresolved. In HCI, Monge Roffarello and De Russis's meta-analysis of digital self-control tools reported a small-to-medium effect on reducing time spent, but noted that the evidence comes mostly from short experiments, often without control groups, that cannot show whether the change lasts. Friction is a design variable worth testing, not a cure.

Two ways to build a content feed

Imagine two versions of the same feed, showing the same posts in the same order. The content is identical. Only the shape of the experience differs.

In Version A, continuous scrolling, new posts appear automatically as the reader nears the bottom of the page. There is no page two, no final post, no visible edge. Reaching the end of what has loaded is never an event, because more has already arrived. The feed never asks whether you want to continue; continuing is simply what happens next. If the reader stops, the decision has to come entirely from them, made against the momentum of the interface.

In Version B, intentional continuation, the feed shows a limited batch of posts, perhaps ten, followed by a visible stopping point: a short note that the batch is finished, a count of how many posts have been seen so far, and an option to load more. Nothing prevents the reader from continuing. The next batch is a single tap away. But the end of the batch becomes a moment, and continuing becomes a choice rather than a default.

That is the essential difference. Version B does not force anyone to stop, impose a time limit or hide content. It restores the kind of decision point that a paginated list or the last page of a magazine once supplied without anyone noticing. In the terms of the previous section, it changes which action costs effort: in Version A, stopping requires initiative; in Version B, continuing does, if only slightly.

Both designs offer access to exactly the same information. What changes is the behavioral environment surrounding it, and the research reviewed above suggests that cues, defaults and stopping points shape behavior in ways that willpower alone does not explain.

This comparison is an illustration, not evidence. Nothing here shows that Version B improves well-being, reduces regret or changes long-term habits. Those are empirical questions, best answered by testing designs like these with real users and measuring the outcomes that matter to them.

Can we measure success differently?

Teams optimize what they measure. Time spent, session length and daily active users are cheap to collect, hard to dispute and tied to revenue. As the Kleinberg model makes explicit, they cannot distinguish a person who stayed because the product was valuable from one who stayed because leaving took effort.

Complementary signals get closer. Task completion asks whether someone who arrived to do something did it. Satisfaction and perceived control, gathered in brief in-product surveys, capture whether the time felt worthwhile. Notification usefulness shows in how often notifications are opened deliberately rather than dismissed or disabled. Voluntary return, sessions started without a prompt, separates a pull the user generates from one the system generates. Reported regret asks directly whether a session was time well spent.

None of these is easy. Surveys suffer from low response rates and selection bias, and regret is colored by mood. Users genuinely disagree: one person's relaxing evening of scrolling is another's lost one. And any metric that becomes a target can be gamed, a well-being metric included.

The practical approach is to treat these as guardrails, not replacements. When an experiment raises session length, check task completion and reported control in the same arms. A change that adds time while lowering perceived control is a different result from one that raises both, even if the headline dashboard cannot tell them apart.

The responsibility of developers

It would be convenient to blame engineers, and wrong. Developers usually implement requirements set elsewhere, under deadlines, against targets and business models they did not choose. Most infinite feeds were built by people trying to make a product feel smooth.

But engineering responsibility has never been limited to intent. We expect developers to consider security risks nobody asked about and accessibility needs missing from the ticket. An interface's behavioral consequences belong in the same category.

In practice that means asking a slightly different question in design review: not only what a feature makes possible, but what it makes easier, more automatic, or harder to interrupt. Engineers can flag metrics that reward behavior users would not endorse. Designers can make stopping points visible. Product managers can propose guardrails. Organizations, which set the incentives, carry the largest share, because individual conscience is a poor substitute for goals that don't penalize doing the right thing.

Designing for the freedom to leave

Engagement and autonomy are not opposites; the best software earns long sessions because people choose them. The problem begins when a system becomes better at keeping people than at serving them, and our metrics cannot tell the difference.

Behavioral science offers no villain here and no simple fix, only a quieter observation: people act within environments, and much of their environment is now made of code. Those who write it are deciding, whether they intend to or not, where the exits are and how easy they are to find.

If we can design software that makes people want to stay, can we also design software that respects their decision to leave?

EyeZen v1.2.0: Bringing Local-First Workspace Customization to the Browser

EyeZen v1.2.0 is officially available!

After building the desktop foundation of EyeZen with Rust, Tauri 2, React and TypeScript, I've reached a new milestone: a functional browser edition with local settings persistence and a dedicated documentation website.

Why a web edition?

EyeZen started as a desktop application focused on workspace personalization, comfort preferences, profiles and break routines.

However, many features—such as changing themes, creating profiles and organizing break reminders—don't require access to native operating-system APIs.

Version 1.2.0 makes these capabilities accessible directly from a browser.

What's new in v1.2.0?

1. EyeZen Web

The browser edition includes ten appearance themes, nine starter workspace profiles, customizable profiles, scheduled routines, break reminders and accessibility preferences.

Users can personalize their environment without installing the desktop application.

2. Persistent local browser settings

A major part of this release involved implementing reliable browser persistence.

EyeZen stores settings locally, validates saved data and handles malformed records rather than silently overwriting them.

Settings can also be exported and imported as JSON.

The web and desktop editions use compatible settings schemas, although synchronization is manual rather than automatic.

3. Permission-aware reminders

EyeZen supports optional in-app break reminders and notification functionality.

Browser notification permission is requested through an explicit user interaction.

Reminders depend on the active application or browser tab and remain subject to browser and operating-system restrictions.

4. A new documentation website

Version 1.2.0 also introduces comprehensive public documentation.

It covers:

  • Application features and configuration
  • Web versus desktop compatibility
  • Installation and setup
  • Privacy and local storage
  • Architecture and accessibility
  • Troubleshooting and frequently asked questions

5. Maintaining honest platform boundaries

The browser edition cannot tint unrelated desktop windows, enumerate physical monitors or change hardware brightness.

The installed desktop application retains optional software-based visual tint overlays on supported environments.

Neither edition claims medical benefits or hardware-level display calibration.

Communicating these differences clearly is important when building trustworthy cross-platform software.

Built with open technologies

The project uses:

  • Rust and Tauri 2 for native desktop functionality
  • React and TypeScript for the interface
  • Vite for web builds
  • GitHub Actions for automated builds and deployment
  • GitHub Pages for the static browser application and documentation

EyeZen is open source under the Mozilla Public License 2.0.

Try EyeZen

Web edition: https://sanskarin.github.io/EyeZen/

Documentation: https://sanskarin.github.io/EyeZen/docs/

GitHub release: https://github.com/sanskarIN/EyeZen/releases/tag/v1.2.0

Source code: https://github.com/sanskarIN/EyeZen

What's next?

EyeZen will continue evolving through better workspace customization, platform compatibility, accessibility improvements and stronger real-device testing.

If you use EyeZen or work with Rust, Tauri, TypeScript or cross-platform applications, I'd welcome your feedback and contributions.

What would you prioritize next for EyeZen?

TL;DR: I ran an experiment with AI-augmented development. In one month we produced 400k+ lines of code, 150 features, 240 fixes and 50 refactors, then the entropy accelerated and the velocity collapsed. What normally takes years of accumulated technical debt across multiple teams happened in weeks.

Hi there, my name is Takah, I'm a Principal Software Engineer from Brazil. In the past months I've been conducting a few experiments on how to adapt our SDLC and explore new ways of working with AI, both enabling non-engineers to code in our repos and also enhancing every guard-rail, guideline and common market standards to support this type of workflow.

What Is Software Entropy?

But let's circle back to the title of this article: what is Software Entropy? First of all, what is entropy? I'll freely give one interpretation that entropy, borrowed from thermodynamics, is the natural tendency toward disorder or uncertainty in a system, and what is exactly software entropy? I'd say its the natural tendency of any given software and system to disorder, when new features are being added, new modules, new fixes, quick-wins, a hacky solution to fix or deliver something in time, or to prevent another incident, regardless of the most architectural pre-definition and future-proof hexagonal multi-flexible, composable and any other blazingly fast buzzword you wanna add, it's impossible to predict and prevent all use-cases beforehand, that's why entropy always end up happening.

Software entropy is not a bug, it's a fundamental property of any system that grows. The question is never if it will happen, its how fast, and whether you have the mechanisms to manage it.

What Does AI Have to Do With Software Entropy?

And what AI has to do with Software Entropy? Like i said one of the experiments i did was me a Software engineer and 2 other designers, which we had the challenge of developing a whole new experience of a chat and we wanted to leverage the AI ecosystem at its maximum.

So first, before any line of code, i aligned the scope, contracts, and overall architecture of the project:

  • Tech stack
  • Repository setup, code structure, architectural guidelines
  • AI guidelines: agents, skills, context files for testing, styling, developing new features, feature-branches

And after the initial setup we had, and helping them setup their own setup with claude, our internal ai-proxy, repository, vpns, etc we started developing. And at the beginning it was awesome. The guidelines and setup were satisfactory, features seemed to be right, we were adding one feature after another with autonomy, tests, coverage, and apparently following the project guidelines.

But whats the problem?

The Turn: Week Three

After 3 weeks we had a codebase with more than 400k lines, dozens of features, animations, micro-interactions that would maybe take several sprints to be made if they were handcrafted by a team of engineers. But at this moment things started to break down:

  • Each feature velocity started to decline
  • New behaviours that interacted with previous states started to skyrocket race-conditions
  • One new feature broke 3 other working ones
  • A simple feature that previously took a few hours now took days

And we had to circle back and analyze what was happening.

The guidelines and guard-rails that were previously added were not enough, because even with a strict guideline saying to our models and setup: "Use X technology or Y Architecture or Z state management tool in this way," the probabilist nature of LLMs still were delusional.

We had several features that reimplemented different state machines, did full animations, sound, charts from scratch while it was already solved in a sibling part of the application, and one of the signs were the codebase growth, it was exponentially growing in number of lines and files.

To give you a sense of the scale, in roughly one month we accumulated:

  • 150 features added
  • 240 fixes applied
  • 50 refactors performed, with refactors as large as removing more than 50k lines of code in a single one

And I'm not alone in this, the data from 2026 tells the same story across the industry. The 2025 DORA State of AI-assisted Software Development report found that a 25% increase in AI adoption is associated with a 7.2% decrease in delivery stability, because AI allows developers to generate code much faster and it often leads to larger batch sizes, which are slower to review and more prone to creating system instability. New Relic's 2026 State of AI Coding report, which surveyed 200 technology leaders, found that while 94% of them rate AI-generated code as higher quality at review time, 78% report more incidents once it ships and 82% experienced at least one production failure tied to AI-generated code in the past six months. They call this agent debt, the rapid accumulation of unvetted architectural logic that triggers production incidents down the line. And a systematic review of 34 studies covering 2,847 developers found that technical debt principal increased by 1.8 person-days per 1,000 AI-generated lines of code, with the debt ratio doubling within 6 months without mitigation.

The Fix: Tightening the Guard-Rails

To fix that we had to do several fixes, refactors, and with each fix and refactor to strictly tighten the guard-rails, tests, and add custom deterministic tools to truly ensure that the code was following each guideline. In practice this meant:

  • AI guard-rails in agents: direct instructions, specific skills and context files that enforced architectural patterns
  • Deterministic tools: lint rules, pipeline validations and custom checks that verified architectural conformance before merge
  • Strict refactoring cycles: regular mandatory refactoring capacity to reduce the debt principal
  • Expert oversight: a specialized developer actively enhancing the guidelines, understanding what to use, what not to use, how to fix, and correcting the AI to follow new strict rules

In the end result the AI usage was a success, within a month we developed something that would take months to be made handcrafted, but at what cost?

If a specialized developer was not present enhancing the guidelines, understanding what to use, what not to use, how to fix, and actively enhancing its guard-rails this codebase was doomed to failure. Or maybe a full refactor or depriorization due to the effort of maintaining it.

The Exponential Decline of the Codebase

So whats my conclusion? All that happening within a month its the same thing i saw happening during years of a codebase, it normally takes months of multiple developers, teams, and technical debts accumulated to reach the same level of entropy and disorder where each new feature was breaking 3 others. What I'm calling the exponential decline of the codebase is not just a metaphor, its what happens when the rate of entropy generation outpaces the rate of human oversight by an order of magnitude.

The IEEE Computer Society puts it bluntly: "Standing between such problematic AI output and other downstream disasters? Software engineers. The value of engineers with the software lifecycle knowledge needed to guide and oversee AI assistants and their output is immeasurable."

The arXiv paper "Beyond the 'Diff'" defines agentic entropy as "a systemic drift that traditional code diff-based and HCXAI methods fail to capture, as they address local outputs rather than global agentic behaviour," and notes that "functional checks (e.g., confirming that the code runs) can thus mask deeper architectural violations and security gaps, producing an illusion of rapid progress while drift accumulates beneath the surface."

The AI era is awesome, but without proper follow-up and deep specialized people understanding whats being written and which software engineering strategies, architecture and design patterns to follow, it will exponentially increase the software entropy. Gartner predicts that by 2029, 60% of organizations will adopt smaller software engineering teams at scale, up from 15% in 2026. But smaller teams with AI does not mean no engineers, it means engineers with different skills, architects, overseers, guard-rail builders. The ACM Technology Policy Council's TechBrief on vibe coding warns that it "often skips over core engineering practices that ensure systems are secure, reliable, and maintainable," and their lead author Simson Garfinkel says it directly: "It's making developers dramatically more effective, but it's also introducing security vulnerabilities, increasing technical debt, and producing code that can be difficult to maintain."

A Reflection for Engineering Leaders

If you're a manager, head of engineering, VP or CTO reading this, i want you to reflect on a few things:

  • How are you aspiring your org to be? Are you designing for a future where AI does the coding and engineers do the oversight, or one where engineers use AI as a tool while retaining architectural ownership?
  • Where are your gaps? Do you have mechanisms to detect software entropy as it accumulates, deterministic guard-rails and not just guidelines, engineers who can recognize when the AI is drifting from architectural intent?
  • Whats your oversight model? The data from New Relic shows that 62% of technology leaders report their teams trust AI-generated code enough to ship it to production without line-by-line manual verification, is that a risk you're willing to take?

My Disclosure on AI

In that way, i don't dislike Agentic Coding, neither the idea of non-engineers coding, my conclusion is that the current state of ai tools are not ready yet to be driven by full Ai enthusiasts, software engineers are going to exist, this is the new normal we should not fear Ai we should embrace these new tools and understand how we could be more productive and have more time to focus in new strategies, features, design patterns, career, our mental and physical health and our familly not only delivering more value to our shareholders.

The illusion that a single person with AI can replace a team of engineers is just that, an illusion. What we experienced in one month is what happens when you remove the expertise from the loop. The entropy accelerates, the velocity collapses, and the cost compounds. Software engineers are still necessary, the question is, are we building organizations that know how to use them?

RepoDNA v1.4.0 is now available.

This release represents a new step in the development of RepoDNA, my open-source, local-first repository intelligence and codebase archaeology project.

Rather than introducing another major analysis subsystem, v1.4.0 focuses on strengthening the application's identity, improving startup behavior, addressing accessibility details, and resolving several usability issues.

The central philosophy remains unchanged:

Understand your codebase. See its DNA.

What is RepoDNA?

RepoDNA helps developers understand software repositories beyond individual source files.

It analyzes information such as:

  • Repository structure and architecture
  • Programming languages and dependencies
  • Git history and repository evolution
  • Code quality and complexity signals
  • Project hotspots and findings
  • Evidence-backed reports and Project DNA cards

It also supports optional AI-assisted explanations grounded in repository analysis.

The goal is to turn complex repositories into information developers can explore, understand, and act on.

1. An original, hand-authored SVG logo

The most visible change in v1.4.0 is RepoDNA's new logo.

The design combines DNA-inspired geometry with code-graph relationships.

It uses a navy, blue, and teal color palette and was created directly from SVG vector geometry rather than AI-generated artwork.

Because the design is vector-based, it can be rendered consistently at different sizes.

The identity is now reflected across the web application, desktop application, PWA icons, and project branding.

A matching vector wordmark was also introduced.

2. A branded startup experience

The new release introduces branded startup screens for the web and desktop applications.

The startup experience is designed to display branding while the application initializes.

Importantly, the implementation does not intentionally delay application startup merely to keep the branding visible.

The objective is to provide a consistent first impression without sacrificing usability.

3. Accessibility improvements

One of the less visible but important fixes involves keyboard focus.

Following application initialization, keyboard focus could fail to move to the main content region after the startup screen had been displayed.

v1.4.0 addresses this transition.

Accessibility improvements like this matter because visual changes should not make the application harder to navigate using a keyboard.

4. More reliable deep links

The web deep-link parser also received a correction.

Previously, additional question marks within URL query values were not preserved correctly in every case.

The updated parser handles these values more reliably.

This is a relatively small change, but correct URL parsing is essential for predictable web application behavior.

5. Documentation and GitHub Action corrections

The documentation was also updated.

In particular, the FAQ previously contained an incorrect statement suggesting that no official GitHub Action existed.

The FAQ now points developers toward the maintained RepoDNA GitHub Action and its documentation.

This makes the integration options clearer for users.

6. Expanded ways to support the project

RepoDNA is an open-source project, and the release introduces PayPal.Me as an additional support option.

The new support link appears alongside existing options in the project documentation and interface.

Support remains entirely optional.

7. Testing and release validation

The release includes regression checks for startup branding and support links.

The release workflow also covers the Rust codebase, WebAssembly components, TypeScript, desktop application, documentation, and dependency advisories.

These checks help maintain consistency across the project's different distribution formats.

What has not changed?

RepoDNA remains focused on local-first development.

The core analysis features continue to function without requiring developers to upload their repositories to a cloud analysis service.

Optional AI capabilities remain separate from the main repository analysis process.

The purpose of RepoDNA is still to help developers understand the structure, evolution, and relationships within their software projects.

Try RepoDNA v1.4.0

The release provides distribution options for Windows, macOS, and Linux, together with command-line, WebAssembly, npm, and container workflows.

You can also explore the web version directly in your browser.

https://github.com/sanskarIN/RepoDNA/releases/tag/v1.4.0

Web Application:

https://sanskarin.github.io/RepoDNA/

Source Code:

https://github.com/sanskarIN/RepoDNA

What's next?

The new visual identity creates a more consistent foundation for future releases.

Future development can continue expanding repository analysis capabilities, improving performance and usability, and refining the experience across platforms.

Feedback is especially valuable from developers working with complex repositories or experimenting with local-first development tools.

If RepoDNA sounds useful, consider exploring the source code, opening an issue, contributing, or sharing your experience.

articles.title: How do you manage CORS for thousands of customer domains? Per tenant, with three answers instead of two
articles.description: Our domain registry can stop answering. It can also answer that a customer's domain is no longer...
articles.body_html:
Our domain registry can stop answering. It can also answer that a customer's domain is no longer allowed. Both cases leave the proxy without a usable current list, but only the first gives us a reason to reuse an older one.

That distinction shaped our per-tenant CORS cache. We keep valid results for 15 minutes and a fallback copy for 24 hours. An authoritative refusal erases that fallback, so the next outage cannot bring a removed domain back.

One domain per customer

At GoodBarber, the web version of each customer app has its own domain, either a platform subdomain or a custom one. We are piloting a proxy that lets widgets call third-party APIs while their private keys stay on the server. Its CORS policy has to fit that domain model, even while the service itself is limited to a small pilot.

Our first static allowlist was manageable for five pilot apps. It could not follow the platform's thousands of domains as customers changed them. Allowing arbitrary origins would also defeat the restriction we wanted; PortSwigger documents that mistake in its guide to CORS misconfigurations. We needed to resolve the list for each tenant.

The preflight does not know who is calling

An actual API call carries a short-lived token naming the tenant. Its preflight arrives earlier, without that token: CORS preflight requests do not carry credentials. We receive an origin, a proposed method and a list of header names, so the token cannot supply the tenant for this lookup.

The request path can. It contains an opaque connector handle belonging to one tenant. We resolve the handle, then the tenant's domains. Because this happens before token validation, the lookup must also tolerate requests from arbitrary callers.

Origins, exactly as a browser sends them

The registry returns a domain. A browser sends an origin, and the comparison is string equality, so the list has to be built the way a browser would write it.

  • The default port for the scheme is omitted: :443 for HTTPS, :80 for HTTP. Non-default ports are kept.
  • A custom domain yields two origins, with and without www, since customers publish both. A subdomain of ours yields exactly one.
  • An internationalised domain is converted to punycode, which is what the browser sends.
  • The response carries the one matching origin and Vary: Origin, as MDN recommends for an explicit origin. Never *, and Origin: null never matches.

A miss needs a reason

Once the main cache entry expires, the registry lookup can produce three different outcomes:

The registry… What the proxy serves What it stores
answers with domains those origins the list for 15 minutes, and a second copy for 24 hours
cannot be reached, answers an error or sends garbage the 24-hour copy, if there is one the main entry again, for 60 seconds
answers clearly that the tenant has no usable domain no CORS headers an empty list for 60 seconds, and it deletes the 24-hour copy

The outage path borrows the idea of stale-if-error. Apps can keep using a previously accepted origin while the registry is unavailable. Caching that fallback decision for 60 seconds reduces repeated lookups; it does not by itself guarantee a global request-rate bound when concurrent misses occur.

An explicit removal has a different meaning. If we kept its old list, a later registry outage could restore the revoked origin from the 24-hour copy. Deleting that copy makes the refusal survive the outage too.

The pre-auth path is bounded

Before any I/O, we check the handle's shape and hash it for use in cache keys. Unknown handles are cached as unknown for 60 seconds. If the shared cache is unavailable, an in-process cache lasting 5 seconds, with at most 4,096 entries, limits repeated database work.

The preflight path responds with 204. If neither the lookup nor its permitted fallback yields an allowed origin, the response omits CORS headers. Dependency errors therefore do not become a 500, and the browser cannot proceed with the cross-origin call after an unsuccessful preflight.

Treat your cache as input

The cache is shared infrastructure, so what comes out of it is validated like anything else that crosses a boundary. Values are JSON, never pickled objects. Every list read back is checked, item by item, against the same pattern that judged it on the way in. A value that exists but fails that check is ignored and logged as a tampering signal.

Review found a mismatch here. Normalisation accepted a hostname containing an underscore, but cache validation used a stricter rule and rejected it. That value would have been repeatedly written, discarded and fetched again, leaving both caches ineffective for the tenant. Applying the same rule on write and read removed the disagreement.

CORS is not the lock

These responses govern browser access. A client such as curl does not enforce them, so actual requests still undergo token validation and the connector's permission checks. Using an older CORS list leaves those checks in place; it changes which browser origins may read the responses.

The feature and its hardening landed on July 23, six minutes apart: the second commit is the adversarial review of the first. The module has 48 tests: normalisation, the three outcomes, the bounds of the pre-auth path, and the few static origins we add on top.

To test the distinction, cache an allowed domain, have the registry explicitly remove it, then make the registry unavailable. The domain should remain absent. Testing an outage alone would miss the case where a cache reverses a decision it had already received.

articles.title: AI Crawler Gets a 403? Trace the Request Before Editing robots.txt
articles.description: When an AI crawler gets a 403 response, find the layer that refused the request before changing...
articles.body_html:
When an AI crawler gets a 403 response, find the layer that refused the request before changing crawler rules. A browser loading the page successfully does not establish that the crawler can fetch it. An allowed robots.txt entry does not explain which security rule handled a later request.

Start with a real request record, its time and the exact URL. Check the edge security event, then the origin response where available. Keep crawler identity separate from a user-agent string someone can copy. The aim is a narrow diagnosis, with the site's intended access policy kept intact.

This guide uses a fictional documentation site to explain the investigation. It does not ask you to disable protections, open private routes or change every bot policy. The examples are teaching scenarios, not tests of HoneyWeRank or reports from Uriel's infrastructure.

Write down the failure precisely

“Claude cannot read our docs” is a starting report, not a complete diagnosis. Which Claude product and mode was used? Was web search active? Did a real request reach your edge? Was the failed address the document itself, a redirect target or a resource needed to display it?

For the fictional site, record a public guide URL, a UTC time and an observed 403. Save the request identifier if the service exposes one. Also record the response body and which system produced it, without copying private headers or credentials into a public issue.

A successful human session may include cookies or a previous challenge result. A crawler has a different request context. Compare those contexts instead of treating the human result as proof that the access report must be wrong.

Use a bounded observation period. A request from last month may have encountered a rule that no longer exists. An event recorded after a deploy may reflect a new configuration. Keep the configuration version or change time beside the evidence so the investigation remains reproducible.

Check the edge event before the application log

If a request was stopped at the edge, an application log may contain no corresponding entry. That absence alone does not prove which edge product stopped it. Look for the matching security event using the recorded time, hostname, path and request identifier.

Cloudflare's AI Crawl Control documentation says unsuccessful crawler requests may result from different rules or response errors. Its table is therefore a starting view, not a complete explanation that the AI blocking action caused every failure.

Inspect the event's action and rule details. Write a short finding such as “The request matched this custom rule and received the configured denial.” That is more useful than “Cloudflare blocks AI,” which turns one observed configuration into a broad claim.

If the edge passed the request onward, continue at the origin. Compare the origin access log and any application response. A route guard, hosting rule or upstream service may be responsible. Keep a category for insufficient evidence rather than assigning the failure to whichever dashboard looks most familiar.

Verify the requester, not just the label

A user-agent string is a claim made in a request. A local request with a crawler's name can be useful for testing how your own matching rule behaves, but it does not prove that the request came from that crawler's operator.

Cloudflare documents that crawler detection on its free plan uses user-agent strings, with more thorough detection available through Bot Management. Do not describe a name match as verified identity when the evidence only supports that simpler classification.

For OpenAI search access, OpenAI's current search guidance points site owners to OAI-SearchBot and published searchbot IP addresses. Check that current provider evidence when investigating an actual OpenAI request. Do not reuse another provider's address list or assume that every agent from one company has the same purpose.

Keep the investigation record explicit: observed user agent, identity evidence checked and any remaining uncertainty. You can establish that your rule rejects a string without establishing that a real search crawler was rejected. Those findings call for different next steps.

Separate access policy from request handling

Before proposing a fix, ask the owner which public content they intend to make available for search or user-directed retrieval. That decision is separate from training access. It is also separate from whether a particular request was handled correctly.

Suppose the fictional site intends to allow a relevant search agent to read public guides. An event shows that a broad custom rule denied a matching request. The next task is to review that rule against the intended policy, not to turn off all bot controls.

Check other public paths and keep private ones outside the investigation's release scope. A diagnosis about a public guide gives no reason to expose account pages, internal previews or authenticated material. The fact that a crawler is useful for discovery does not make it entitled to every route.

Treat any proposed exception as a change requiring the site's normal review. Identify the intended requester, paths and remaining controls. Record the exact reason for the change and how the team will tell whether it worked. This guide explains how to prepare that review; it is not a blanket instruction to create an allow rule.

Work through three different failures

In the first fictional case, the edge event identifies an intentional AI Crawl Control block. The response matches that policy. There is no technical defect established yet. The owner needs to decide whether the policy still matches their publishing goals.

In the second case, the agent appears allowed in one view, but a different custom security rule denies the same request. The diagnosis is a conflict between the intended treatment and the rule that actually ran. Save the event details before recommending a narrow correction.

In the third case, the edge passes the request, while the application returns an error because the public route expects a browser session. The work belongs with the route or hosting behavior. Editing the crawler's robots.txt group would not explain or repair that application response.

These cases can look identical in a screenshot of the failed fetch. Their remedies differ because the evidence differs. The useful troubleshooting output is the responsible layer and policy, not simply a list of switches someone might try.

Retest the same question after a change

Once an approved change is made, repeat a comparable request and record the new time and configuration. Check the response status and the returned document. A 200 response containing a challenge, empty shell or unrelated page is not the same as receiving the guide's useful content.

If a provider's actual request cannot be observed, state that limit. A controlled local check may validate your own rule logic. It should not become a claim that a real provider has successfully crawled or indexed the page.

Keep an easy comparison between the old and new evidence: exact URL, responsible layer, rule, response and returned content. Remove secrets from screenshots or exports before sharing them. A clear issue can be brief while still carrying enough detail for another engineer to follow.

Watch for recurrence across a small set of representative public paths. One repaired guide may reveal a rule that affects a whole documentation section. That is a reason to test the relevant pattern, not to assume that every page or every AI agent now works.

Stop the diagnosis at the right boundary

Successful access is one prerequisite for some discovery workflows. It is not proof of indexing, retrieval, a linked citation or a brand recommendation. OpenAI's documentation expressly says search placement is not guaranteed.

After access is established, evaluate the next question with its own evidence. Is the page discoverable? Does it answer a useful query? Does an observed answer cite it accurately? Avoid changing five unrelated parts of the site because a single response still does not mention the brand.

Close the incident with a specific statement: the request failed at a named layer, the reviewed change addressed that cause, and the retest showed a defined result. List what remains unknown. That gives the content team a trustworthy starting point for the next visibility check.

articles.title: Stop Electing a Leader Tab. SharedWorker Just Holds the Connection.
articles.description: Electing a leader tab to own one shared WebSocket works great — until the leader is the tab someone closes. SharedWorker skips the election: the connection lives in the worker, not in any tab, so there's no leader to lose.
articles.body_html:
Last week's fix for "six tabs, six WebSockets" was navigator.locks: elect one tab as leader, let it hold the one real connection, relay everything to the rest over BroadcastChannel. It works. I said as much at the time.

It also has a seam I didn't dwell on: the connection lives inside a tab. Close that tab — the user's doing, not a bug — and the lock releases, a new leader gets picked within the same event loop turn, and that new leader still has to open a brand-new WebSocket from scratch. Real handshake, real round trip, real gap before updates resume. For a dashboard, nobody notices. For a live price ticker or a shared cursor, that gap is the whole ballgame.

There's a version of this where no tab ever owns the connection, so no tab closing can take it away.

The belief: something has to own the socket

The leader-election pattern isn't wrong. It's the correct answer to a real constraint: a WebSocket object lives in some JavaScript execution context, and until recently the only context every tab could reliably reach was another tab's. So you pick one, crown it leader, and accept that leadership — like any job held by one person — has a handoff cost when that person leaves.

// what every tab currently runs
navigator.locks.request("app-connection-leader", () => {
  const socket = new WebSocket("wss://example.com/live");
  socket.onmessage = (e) => channel.postMessage(e.data);
  return new Promise(() => {}); // held until this tab closes
});

This is fine code. It's also solving "how do we share one connection" by picking which page gets to be the exception — which means the exception goes away the moment that page does.

The context that outlives every tab

A SharedWorker is a separate execution context, like a regular Worker, except more than one tab can connect to the same instance of it at once. The browser starts it the first time any tab asks for it by URL, keeps it running as long as at least one tab is still connected, and every tab talks to it through its own MessagePort — a direct, two-way pipe into one shared scope that was never inside any of their tabs to begin with.

// live-feed-worker.js
let socket;
const ports = new Set();

self.onconnect = (event) => {
  const port = event.ports[0];
  ports.add(port);

  if (!socket) {
    socket = new WebSocket("wss://example.com/live");
    socket.onmessage = (e) => {
      for (const p of ports) p.postMessage(e.data);
    };
  }

  port.onmessage = (e) => socket.send(e.data); // tab -> server, through the one socket
};

// every tab, on load
const worker = new SharedWorker("/live-feed-worker.js");
worker.port.onmessage = (e) => renderUpdate(e.data);

That's the whole wiring. No election, because there's nothing to elect a leader for — the worker opens the socket once, the first time ports.size goes from zero to one, and every tab after that just gets handed a port into a worker that's already running. Close the tab that happened to open first, second, or fifth: socket doesn't move, because it was never that tab's to carry.

One detail worth getting right: setting port.onmessage directly starts the port automatically. You only need an explicit port.start() call if you wire the port with addEventListener("message", …) instead — the implicit start only fires off the property setter.

🎮 Try it yourself

▶️ Open the interactive playground →

Runs right in your browser — poke at it and watch the concept react live.

The puzzle this trades in

Removing the leader doesn't remove every problem — it swaps one for a quieter one. navigator.locks tells you, immediately and for free, the moment a tab is gone: the lock releases the instant the tab closes, crashes, or navigates away, because the browser is the one holding the lock and the browser knows. A SharedWorker gets no such notice. There is no standard "this port just disconnected" event — a port left behind by a closed tab just sits in your Set, reachable only by postMessage calls that go nowhere, until the browser eventually garbage-collects it on its own schedule.

That's invisible at first — a few dead ports costs you nothing but a wasted loop iteration — but it means you can't use "how many ports do I have" as a live headcount, and you can't reliably ask "is anyone still connected" to decide when to close the real socket. The fix is the same one people have used since shared workers existed: don't wait to be told, say so on the way out.

// every tab
addEventListener("pagehide", () => {
  worker.port.postMessage({ type: "closing" });
});

// live-feed-worker.js
port.onmessage = (e) => {
  if (e.data?.type === "closing") {
    ports.delete(port);
    if (ports.size === 0) socket.close();
    return;
  }
  socket.send(e.data);
};

Two extra lines on each side, and now the worker's idea of "who's connected" matches reality closely enough to act on — close the real socket once the last tab says goodbye, instead of leaving it open for a page that's already gone.

Browser support, honestly

Desktop Chrome, Firefox, and Edge have supported SharedWorker for a very long time, and Safari added it in version 16 — including iOS Safari 16, which is the gap that used to rule this API out for anything mobile-facing. The one real asterisk: Chrome for Android didn't support SharedWorker at all for years, specifically because of unpredictable process-lifecycle behavior on mobile, and only gained support in a 2026 release. If a meaningful slice of your traffic is Android Chrome on an older version, check caniuse.com's current numbers against your own analytics before you rely on this being universal — and keep last week's navigator.locks pattern in your back pocket as the fallback that works everywhere today, Android included.

No leader, no handoff, one quieter problem instead

The leader-election pattern isn't obsolete — it's still the one answer that works on every browser shipping today, and it's still the right call if your Android numbers say you can't assume SharedWorker yet. But where it's available, it removes the actual thing that made leader election necessary: a connection that has to live inside some tab's lifetime. A SharedWorker's connection lives in its own context, outside every tab equally, so closing any one of them — including the tab that happened to open it first — costs nothing at all.

Go check whether your app's "shared" state actually lives independently of every tab, or just inside whichever one got there first. What's the oldest "pick a tab to be special" hack you're still running?

articles.title: Keeping declarativeNetRequest rules in sync after a Manifest V3 service worker restarts
articles.description: By mid-afternoon, my Chrome usually had 40+ tabs open across three windows. I tried several tab...
articles.body_html:
By mid-afternoon, my Chrome usually had 40+ tabs open across three windows. I tried several tab managers, but they either demanded a cloud account, locked basic features behind a subscription, or only solved one half of the problem.

So I spent the last few months building my own: PYLON, an offline-first New Tab that pairs project tab workspaces with dev tools and a deep-focus Pomodoro timer.

This post is about one specific engineering challenge: the site blocker.

The hardest part wasn’t intercepting requests — it was deciding what the source of truth should be when a Manifest V3 background service worker constantly terminates and restarts.

The setup

When a focus session starts, the extension redirects configured distraction sites to a local focus-intercept.html page bundled inside the extension.

I chose Chrome's modern declarativeNetRequest (DNR) API over old blocking webRequests so that the browser itself evaluates rules at native speed without injecting custom JavaScript into the request path.

Three pieces of state have to stay consistent:

What Where it lives Why
Blocked domains chrome.storage.local Survives restarts, handles crashes, easily exported
Active redirect rules DNR Dynamic Rules Evaluated directly by the browser network stack
Rule IDs A reserved ID range (1000–1999) Ensures we only delete focus rules without touching other extension rules

My core rule: chrome.storage.local is the sole source of truth. DNR rules are merely a temporary mirror of it.

Step 1: Clean and normalize user input

Users paste whatever happens to be in their address bar:

  • https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=...
  • reddit.com/r/webdev
  • x.com:443

Because DNR rules match against hostname patterns (typically using ||domain.com^), passing raw URLs will break rule matching. Every entry must be cleaned to a bare domain before touching storage:

const cleaned = Array.from(new Set((domains || [])
  .map(d => String(d || '').trim().toLowerCase()
    .replace(/^https?:\/\//, '')   // drop the protocol
    .replace(/\/.*$/, '')          // drop any trailing path
    .split(':')[0].split('?')[0])  // drop port numbers and query parameters
  .filter(Boolean)));

Step 2: Rebuild the rules — don't patch them

My initial instinct was incremental updates: add a rule when a user adds a domain, remove one when deleted.

In Manifest V3, incremental patching is an anti-pattern.

Service workers can terminate at any point of idle time. If an event wakes the worker while a write is resolving, or if two storage events trigger simultaneously, incremental updates can leave stale, orphaned rule IDs in the browser engine.

Instead, I adopted an idempotent reconciliation pattern:

  1. Read existing dynamic rules.
  2. Filter for rule IDs belonging to my reserved range.
  3. In a single atomic updateDynamicRules() call, delete all stale IDs and re-apply fresh rules generated from storage.
  4. Retry with backoff if Chrome's internal database locks. 
async function reconcileDnrWithStorage(expectedDomains, retryCount = 0) {
  try {
    const existing = await chrome.declarativeNetRequest.getDynamicRules();
    const staleIds = existing
      .map(r => r.id)
      .filter(id => id >= FOCUS_RULE_ID_START && id <= FOCUS_RULE_ID_END);

    await chrome.declarativeNetRequest.updateDynamicRules({
      removeRuleIds: staleIds,
      addRules: buildShieldRules(expectedDomains || [])
    });
  } catch (e) {
    if (retryCount < 3) {
      await new Promise(r => setTimeout(r, 500));
      await reconcileDnrWithStorage(expectedDomains, retryCount + 1);
    }
  }
}

If the focus session ends, passing an empty array automatically clears all rules in that range.

Step 3: Sweeping already-open tabs

One gotcha with declarativeNetRequest: redirect rules only apply to new network requests.

If a user already has YouTube open in a tab and starts a focus sprint, that tab remains accessible until they click a link or refresh.

To make the block instant, the activation sequence performs a quick tab sweep right after reconciling DNR rules:

const tabs = await chrome.tabs.query({});
for (const tab of tabs) {
  if (tab.url && isDomainBlocked(tab.url, expectedDomains)) {
    chrome.tabs.update(tab.id, { 
      url: chrome.runtime.getURL('focus-intercept.html') 
    });
  }
}

Questions for other extension developers:

Building on Manifest V3 has been an interesting exercise in distributed-systems thinking inside a single browser:

  1. Retry Strategy: Is a static 500ms delay sufficient for DNR rule updates, or have you found exponential backoff necessary under heavy browser load?
  2. Reconciliation Frequency: Do you reconcile DNR rules on every service worker startup (chrome.runtime.onStartup), or strictly when storage change listeners fire?
  3. Race Condition Testing: Has anyone established a reliable local testing setup for simulating abrupt service worker termination during active DNR writes?

If you've tackled DNR sync differently, I’d love to hear your approach in the comments.
